title: "Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/01-files/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](01-files-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Today's biological question

Did seedlings grow differently after a treatment? Before we calculate anything,
we need to know which measurements belong to which plant and where those
measurements are saved. A useful analysis starts with finding the right file.

Our measurements are **simulated teaching data**, not observations from an actual
experiment. Imagine 24 seedlings, each in its own pot. Twelve pots received a
treatment and twelve were controls. We measured each plant at the beginning and
end. The treatment was assigned randomly. A control is a comparison group: it
helps us judge what might have happened without the treatment.

Today you will download the course files, identify a table of measurements, and
find your work again after closing every window. No programming is needed.

## A file is different from the application that opens it

A **file** is a saved collection of information with a name. A photograph, a
table of measurements, and a written report can each be files. An
**application** is a program that opens or changes files. The same table can be
opened by several applications.

For example, `seedlings.csv` is a file. Excel, a text editor, and R can all read
it. Closing Excel does not delete the saved file. Deleting the saved file is a
different action. A file can also exist without any application displaying it.

A **folder**, also called a directory, groups files and other folders. Your
computer's **file system** organises these folders and records where files are
stored. You can explore it using **File Explorer** on Windows or **Finder** on
Mac. A browser such as Firefox or Safari displays websites; it is a different
application from the file manager.

## Download and locate the course folder

1. Download [the course files](../downloads/course-files.zip).
2. Open the browser's downloads list. Use its option to show the download in
   File Explorer or Finder. Notice the folder's name, usually **Downloads**.
3. Find `course-files.zip`. A ZIP archive is a package containing files and
   folders. On Windows, right-click it and choose **Extract All**. On Mac,
   double-click it to extract it. If the browser already extracted it, locate
   the resulting folder instead.
4. Find the extracted folder called `introcomputing-course`. Move this ordinary
   folder into **Documents** using the file manager. Work in this extracted folder.
5. Open `introcomputing-course`. You should see a `data` folder, an `output`
   folder, a `reports` folder, `report.Rmd`, and `introcomputing.Rproj`.
6. Open `data` and find `seedlings.csv`. Keep this file unchanged.

Your computer may have a cloud-managed Documents folder. Tell the teacher if it
does: we will check that your course files are actually available on the laptop,
including when the network is disconnected. A shortcut or a cloud icon is not
the same thing as a complete local copy.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## I see two course folders. Which should I use?

Extraction can create an extra outer folder. Open folders until you find the one
that directly contains `data`, `output`, and `introcomputing.Rproj`. That is the
project folder. Move that whole folder together. Ask for help if filenames end
in `(1)` because you downloaded several copies; choose one working copy rather
than guessing between them later.
:::

## Reading names and extensions

The final part of a filename, such as `.csv` or `.jpg`, is its **extension**.
It gives a clue about the format of the saved information. A CSV is a text table
in which commas separate values. Changing the name `seedlings.csv` to
`seedlings.jpg` would not turn measurements into a photograph.

Make extensions visible. In Windows File Explorer, look for **View → Show →
File name extensions**; older versions place the checkbox directly under View.
In Finder, use **Settings → Advanced → Show all filename extensions**.
Menu wording can vary. Ask for help if you cannot find the setting.

## Open a copy in two ways

1. Copy `data/seedlings.csv` and paste the copy into `output`.
2. Rename the copy `seedlings-practice.csv`. Confirm that it still ends in `.csv`.
3. Open this practice copy. If a spreadsheet opens automatically, notice its
   rows and columns, then close it **without saving changes**.
4. Right-click the practice file and choose **Open with** a text editor, such as
   Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on Mac. Close it without saving changes.

The first lines should contain the following information:

```text
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
P02,control,24.3,32.3
```

The first line is a **header** naming the columns. The next line describes plant
P01. Its initial length was 25.7 millimetres and its final length was 44.3
millimetres. A spreadsheet displays the commas as column boundaries; the text
editor displays the commas themselves. Both applications opened the same file.

Did P01 grow by 44.3 mm, or did it end at 44.3 mm? Its increase was
44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. Keeping the meaning and units of a measurement matters
as much as knowing how to open its file.

## Save a note you can find again

Open a plain-text editor and describe what a row represents,
what the length units are, and where the original measurements are stored. Use
**Save As** and save the note as `day01-notes.txt` in `reports`.

On Mac, choose **Format → Make Plain Text** in TextEdit before saving. On either
system, check the resulting filename in the file manager. It should not secretly
end in `.txt.txt` or `.rtf`.

Close the editor and all file-manager windows. Open the file manager again and
navigate from Documents to your note. Open it. If you can only find it through
an application's “recent files” list, repeat the folder route once more.


## Build a record you can audit


Work in the graphical file manager and a plain-text editor. Keep original
measurements under `data` and practice copies under `output`.

1. Create `reports/file-audit.txt`. In it, record the project folder's name and
   the route you take to reach it from Documents. Include the computer you are
   using; the name of the application alone is not an address.
2. In the file manager, inspect `data/seedlings.csv`, `report.Rmd`, and
   `introcomputing.Rproj`. Record each full filename and its extension. Use the
   type or kind column, where available, to distinguish a folder from a file.
   Explain why `data` is a folder although it has no filename extension.
3. Open `data/seedlings.csv` in the text editor without changing it. Copy its
   **header line** and the P01 record into your audit note. Label the copied lines
   as a description, not a replacement dataset. Write the meaning of all four
   fields in P01's record, including the millimetre units.
4. Copy `output/seedlings-practice.csv` to another practice file named
   `output/name-test.txt`. Open it as plain text. Do you still see commas and the
   same plant measurements? Rename that copy `name-test.csv` again. Record the
   observation: changing the extension changes the name, not the saved information.
5. Open `reports/file-audit.txt`, add today's progress, and save explicitly.
   Close the editor. Locate and reopen the note from the file manager rather
   than from a recent-files list. Check that the last sentence is present. If
   it is absent, investigate whether you saved another copy or an unexpected
   extension before writing the sentence again.
6. Close all windows and follow the route written in your note. Revise any
   instruction that does not identify a folder or file clearly.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: comparing names is easier when extensions are visible

The file manager may hide extensions even while a text editor displays them.
Show them before deciding that two names are identical. A name such as
`file-audit.txt.rtf` is a formatted document, not the plain-text note requested.
Use the editor's plain-text mode and Save As, then inspect the resulting file
again.
:::

## Receive a second measurement file

The new `data/seedlings-transfer.csv` is another
**simulated** study: 18 separate potted seedlings, nine randomly assigned to each
of `control` and `treated`, with initial and final lengths seven days apart.
Its columns have the same definitions as the first seedling table.

1. Locate this second file and make a copy called
   `output/transfer-inspection.csv`. State in your audit which remains the
   original. Open the copy in a text editor and find its header and first record.
2. Find T01: initial length 25.3 mm and final length 40.3 mm. Write a
   sentence saying what was measured. Compute the increase by ordinary arithmetic
   and explain why 40.3 mm is not the increase. Put your answer in the note.
3. Inspect T18 near the end of the file. Record its treatment and two lengths,
   and record where you found it. The table has one header and 18 plant records.
4. In `reports/transfer-receipt.txt`, record:
   source filename, copy filename, number of plants stated in the study, length
   units, and the difference between initial length, final length, and change.
   Include a sentence explaining that these numbers are teaching data.
5. Close the applications and recover both the receipt and the practice copy.
   Confirm that the original filenames under `data` remain as supplied. Explain
   why a screenshot of a table would be harder to update or calculate from than
   the ordinary CSV. A screenshot may help show a problem; it does not replace
   the measurement file.

**Check and retain:** T01's increase is 15.0 mm. T18 is treated, 21.6 mm initially
and 43.0 mm finally. Keep the notes and practice copies, with the original input
and your interpretation in separate files.


## Check your understanding

Try answering before opening the explanation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Does closing an application delete the file? What did copying create?

Closing an application does not delete a saved file. Copying created another
file. Changes to your practice copy would not automatically change the original.
Neither copy is protected against losing the computer if both are stored only
on that computer.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why keep `data/seedlings.csv` unchanged?

It is our starting record. Later we will describe changes in code so that someone
else can repeat the analysis and see what happened to the original measurements.
:::

**Save today:** `reports/day01-notes.txt` and `output/seedlings-practice.csv`.
Be ready to show their locations without relying on “recent files”.
